paragraphs: Indians abroad send home $135 billion a year. Your friend sends photos.
Swipe to read →
Remitly. Western Union. Every bank. They all fight for that money every single month, and none of them care about the friend.
Most of them say "zero fee" and earn on the exchange rate instead. Wise is the rare one that shows its fee upfront.
And slowly, you stop being part of each other's day. No random calls. Just "we should catch up", moved to next weekend. Again.
Your good news reaches them while they sleep. Their bad news reaches you a day late. The friendship now runs on a delay.
Then they come home for three weeks. Family gets every evening. You get one dinner, and you'll take it.
No one is wrong here. They went where the salary was, and you stayed where the family is. It still hurts.
**The money comes home every month. Your friend comes home once a year.**

end.save: read it before their next visit home.

6045c476e395d4f4d321806532f2d097592c9efd.actual_mechanism: India is the world's top remittance recipient, with the World Bank putting 2024 inflows at roughly $129–138 billion, so the ~$135 billion figure is within the credible range and not demonstrably false. Banks genuinely court NRI money through NRE/NRO accounts and remittance services, and matrimony platforms like Shaadi.com do maintain explicit NRI/location filters and dedicated NRI bride/groom sections. The post's leap — that these systems are 'designed to extract rather than bring them back' and therefore 'reduce' the friendship to visiting hours — is a reading of motive and a generalization about relationships, i.e. opinion, not a falsifiable claim about how a product or market works.

6cdd89336ff7d480f2e38b1c10229aa4827da658.broken_premise: Slide 3: "The apps say 'zero fee'. They earn on the exchange rate instead" — applied to the named set that leads with Wise. This states something demonstrably untrue about how Wise's price is set. Wise does not advertise 'zero fee'; it charges a visible upfront fee and converts at the mid-market (Google) rate with near-zero exchange-rate markup. So for the headline-named provider, both halves of the claim are false. Remitly and banks do fit the 'zero fee / earn on the rate' description; Wise is the counterexample the slide names first.
6cdd89336ff7d480f2e38b1c10229aa4827da658.actual_mechanism: India is indeed the world's top remittance recipient (~$129B in 2024, ~$151B in 2025, so a ~$135B framing is fair), and Wise, Remitly and banks do compete hard for it. But monetization differs by provider: Remitly and most banks bury a 0.5–3% margin in the exchange rate and can thus headline 'zero fee', whereas Wise does the opposite — it uses the real mid-market rate and makes its money from a separate, stated fee, which is its entire market position. Lumping Wise into 'they hide it in the rate' inverts how its price actually works.

Wise is the only provider in our data charging close to zero markup — it makes money entirely through its upfront fee.
Remitly advertises 'zero fee' for bank-funded transfers over $500, but the exchange rate markup (0.5-3.0%) is the real cost of each transfer — this is how Remitly generates revenue.

a13ef4468cede8d4b666ed6a09b40cda90e61629.actual_mechanism: Wise uses the mid-market exchange rate (the real Reuters/Google rate with no markup) and charges a separate, disclosed fee, so its entire cost is shown upfront. Western Union and Remitly offer 'zero fee' options but build their margin into the exchange rate instead — Remitly adds roughly 0.5–3% over mid-market and Western Union roughly 2–4% — so the real cost is hidden in a worse rate. The post's distinction is accurate: Wise is the transparent exception; most rivals disguise cost as a rate markup.

sources.quote: Wise uses the mid-market rate — the same one you'd find on Google or Reuters — with no markup added on top, while Western Union makes money through exchange rate markups.
Remitly makes money in two ways: through fees charged for its money transfer service and through a small percentage margin added to the mid-market rate.
Remitly's Economy service typically doesn't charge a transfer fee, but the exchange rate markup (0.5-3.0%) is the real cost of each transfer — so a 'zero fee' quote can still cost more.

cover.headline: Indians abroad send home $135 billion a year. Your friend sends [photos].
cover.sub: And you know exactly which friend this is.

paragraphs: Indians abroad send home $135 billion a year. Your friend sends photos.
Swipe to read →
Snow. A new apartment. The first car with the steering on the left.
You send back rain and a cutting chai. You're both saying the same thing: I'm fine.
They come home for three weeks, and every evening is booked by family.
You get one dinner to catch up on a whole year.
The friendship didn't end. It got visiting hours.
Call it the visa friendship. Same love, fixed schedule.
And everything around them is built for the money, not the person.
The bank wants their transfers. The matrimony app has an NRI filter. Nothing is built to bring them back.
At some point you stopped asking "when are you coming back?"
Now you ask "when are you visiting?"
Nobody left anybody. They went where the salary was. You stayed where the family is.
Both of you chose right.
**The money comes home every month. Your friend comes home when the leave allows.**

end.send: Send to that friend. Yes, at their 3am.
end.save: Read it before their next visit home.
